title: Sequence Models: RNNs and LSTMs
description: Recurrent networks, backpropagation through time, the vanishing gradient problem, LSTM and GRU gating, and encoder–decoder models.
overview: Text, speech, music, sensor readings and stock prices are sequences: the order matters and the length varies. A fully connected network needs a fixed input size and treats each position separately, so it must learn the same pattern again for every position. A convolutional network sees only a fixed window.

A recurrent neural network (RNN) reads a sequence one element at a time while carrying a hidden state, a running summary of everything seen so far. The same weights are used at every step, in the same spirit as weight sharing in a CNN. This chapter develops the RNN, explains why it forgets, and presents the gated variants (LSTM, GRU) that fixed the problem and dominated sequence modeling before attention took over.
objectives: Write the update of a simple RNN and unroll it through time.
Explain backpropagation through time and why gradients vanish or explode in recurrent networks.
Write the LSTM and GRU equations and explain how gates protect information.
Describe language modeling, perplexity and sampling.
Describe the encoder–decoder architecture and its bottleneck, which motivates attention.

sections.title: Recurrent neural networks
body: Given inputs x₁, …, x_T, a **recurrent neural network** keeps a **hidden state** h_t that is updated at every step from the new input and the previous state, and may emit an output:

eq: h_t = tanh( W_hh h_{t−1} + W_xh x_t + b_h ),    h₀ = 0

body: The same matrices W_hh, W_xh and W_hy are used at every time step. The number of parameters is independent of the sequence length: with hidden size H and input size D, the recurrent layer has H(H + D + 1) parameters (256 hidden and 128 inputs give 98,560).

example.title: A scalar RNN forgets
example.problem: A one-unit RNN has h_t = tanh(0.5 h_{t−1} + x_t) with h₀ = 0. The input is x = (1, 0, 0). Compute h₁, h₂, h₃.
example.solution: h₁ = tanh(1) = 0.762. h₂ = tanh(0.5 · 0.762) = tanh(0.381) = 0.363. h₃ = tanh(0.5 · 0.363) = tanh(0.182) = 0.180. The input at t = 1 still affects the state but fades by about half per step.

list: **Many-to-one**: read a sequence and output one label from the final state (sentiment of a review).
**One-to-many**: generate a sequence from a single input (a caption from an image).
**Many-to-many, aligned**: one output per input (tagging each word with its part of speech).
**Many-to-many, unaligned** (sequence-to-sequence): read a sequence, then write another of a different length (translation).
A **bidirectional** RNN runs a second RNN backward and concatenates the states, so each position has access to both past and future context (when the whole sequence is available).

sections.title: Backpropagation through time
body: To train an RNN, unroll it and apply backpropagation to the unrolled graph. This is **backpropagation through time** (BPTT). Because the weights are shared, the gradient of each weight matrix is the sum of its contributions over all time steps. The gradient from a loss at step T to an early hidden state is a product of Jacobians,

This is the same long product as in the deep feedforward case, but here it is a product of the same matrix many times. Its size behaves like the T − k power of the largest singular value of W_hh (times the derivative of tanh, at most 1). If that value is below 1 the gradient vanishes exponentially, and if above 1 it explodes.

example.title: How fast do gradients decay?
example.problem: In a scalar RNN with recurrent weight w, ignore the activation derivative. How large is ∂h_{10}/∂h₁ for w = 0.5, w = 1 and w = 1.5?
example.solution: The product has 9 factors of w. For w = 0.5, 0.5⁹ = 0.002. For w = 1, 1. For w = 1.5, 1.5⁹ = 38.4. Over 50 steps the same weights give 10⁻¹⁵ and 6 × 10⁸.

list: **Exploding gradients** are handled by **gradient clipping**: if ‖g‖ exceeds a threshold, rescale it to the threshold.

**Vanishing gradients** mean that the network cannot learn dependencies spanning many steps: an RNN can use what happened a few steps ago, but it has trouble connecting a word to a word 50 steps earlier. Gated architectures were designed to address this.
**Truncated BPTT** backpropagates only through the last K steps and carries the hidden state forward without gradient, limiting memory and time for long sequences.

**Teacher forcing**: when training a model that generates sequences, feed it the true previous token rather than its own earlier output. It speeds up and stabilizes training but creates a mismatch with generation (exposure bias).

check.q: Why do the weights of an RNN receive gradient contributions from every time step?
check.a: The same weights are used at every step, so the total gradient is the sum over steps
wrong: Each step has its own weights
The hidden state is reset at each step

sections.title: LSTM and GRU
body: The **long short-term memory** network (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) adds a separate **cell state** c_t that acts as a conveyor belt for information. Learned gates, each a sigmoid between 0 (block) and 1 (pass), control what is written to, kept in and read from the cell. With input x_t and previous state (h_{t−1}, c_{t−1}):

eq: f_t = σ(W_f [h_{t−1}, x_t] + b_f)    forget gate
i_t = σ(W_i [h_{t−1}, x_t] + b_i)    input gate
g_t = tanh(W_g [h_{t−1}, x_t] + b_g)    candidate values
o_t = σ(W_o [h_{t−1}, x_t] + b_o)    output gate

body.key: The cell update c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t−1} + i_t ⊙ g_t is additive. The gradient ∂c_t/∂c_{t−1} = f_t is a gate, not a repeated multiplication by a weight matrix. If the forget gate stays near 1, the gradient flows back across many steps without vanishing. This is the same idea as the residual connection in ResNet.

example.title: One LSTM cell update for a single unit
example.problem: Previous cell state c_{t−1} = 2. The gates are f = 0.9, i = 0.5, o = 0.7 and the candidate g = 0.8. Compute c_t and h_t.
example.solution: c_t = 0.9(2) + 0.5(0.8) = 1.8 + 0.4 = 2.2. h_t = 0.7 · tanh(2.2) = 0.7 · 0.976 = 0.683. Most of the old cell value is kept (f near 1) and a small amount of new information is added.

body: The **gated recurrent unit** (Cho et al., 2014) merges the cell and hidden state and uses two gates, an update gate z_t and a reset gate r_t:

The GRU has three weight matrices instead of the LSTM's four, so it is smaller and a little faster, and it performs similarly on most tasks. An LSTM layer with hidden size H and input size D has 4H(H + D + 1) parameters, four times a simple RNN's: for H = 256 and D = 128 that is 394,240.

body.tip: Initialize the forget gate bias to about 1, so the LSTM starts out remembering, and clip gradients at a norm of 1 to 5.

sections.title: Language modeling
body: A **language model** assigns probabilities to sequences of tokens. Using the chain rule of probability,

body.eq: P(w₁, …, w_T) = Π_t P(w_t | w₁, …, w_{t−1})

body: so the model's job is to predict the next token from all the preceding ones. An **n-gram** model estimates P(w_t | previous n − 1 words) by counting, and fails because most long word sequences never occur in the training data. An RNN conditions on the whole history through its hidden state.

Text is split into **tokens** (words or, more often, subword pieces such as 'un', 'believ', 'able', which keep the vocabulary a manageable size and handle new words). Each token is mapped to a dense vector, a **word embedding**, by a learned lookup table. Embeddings place related words near each other (in word2vec-style embeddings, 'king' − 'man' + 'woman' lies near 'queen'), and they are trained together with the rest of the model or pretrained on large corpora.

At each position the RNN output passes through a softmax over the vocabulary, and the loss is the cross-entropy of the true next token, which is the negative log of the model's probability for it. The standard evaluation measure is **perplexity**, the exponential of the average cross-entropy:

body.eq: perplexity = exp( −(1/T) Σ_t ln P(w_t | w_{<t}) )

body: Perplexity is the effective number of equally likely choices the model sees at each step. An average cross-entropy of 3.0 nats gives a perplexity of e³ = 20: the model is as uncertain as if it chose among 20 equally likely words. Lower is better.

To generate, sample a token from the output distribution, feed it back as the next input, and repeat. Dividing the logits by a **temperature** T before the softmax controls randomness: T < 1 sharpens the distribution (more predictable text), T > 1 flattens it (more varied and more erratic), and T → 0 picks the most likely token. Other strategies are greedy decoding, beam search (keep the k best partial sequences) and top-k or nucleus sampling (sample only among the most likely tokens).

example.title: Temperature
example.problem: Logits for three tokens are (2, 1, 0). Compute the probabilities for T = 1 and T = 0.5.
example.solution: T = 1: (0.665, 0.245, 0.090). T = 0.5: the logits become (4, 2, 0) with exp = (54.6, 7.39, 1), sum 62.99, giving (0.867, 0.117, 0.016). The lower temperature concentrates the probability on the top token.

sections.title: Encoder–decoder models
body: Translation and summarization map one sequence to another of a different length. A **sequence-to-sequence** model (Sutskever et al., 2014) has two RNNs. An **encoder** reads the source sentence and compresses it into a final hidden state, the context vector. A **decoder** starts from that vector and generates the target sentence one token at a time, each token conditioned on the previous ones. Training uses teacher forcing and the cross-entropy of the true target tokens.

list: At generation time the decoder produces a distribution over the vocabulary at each step. **Greedy decoding** takes the most likely token. **Beam search** keeps the B best partial sequences by total log-probability, which finds better outputs than greedy decoding.
A special end-of-sequence token tells the decoder when to stop.

body: A single fixed-size vector must summarize the entire source sentence, however long. Quality degrades quickly for long inputs. The remedy, **attention** (Bahdanau et al., 2014), lets the decoder look back at all the encoder's hidden states at every step and focus on the relevant ones. The next chapter develops attention, and shows that it can replace recurrence altogether.

body.note: Recurrent models process tokens one after another, so they cannot use the parallelism of modern hardware, and training long sequences is slow. Transformers removed both the recurrence and its limits, and replaced LSTMs in most language applications. RNNs remain useful for small models, streaming data and on-device inference, and related state-space models (for example Mamba) revisit recurrence with better properties.

summary: An RNN keeps a hidden state h_t = tanh(W_hh h_{t−1} + W_xh x_t + b), applying the same weights at every step, so its size does not depend on the sequence length.
BPTT unrolls the network. The gradient to early states is a product of Jacobians that vanishes or explodes exponentially in the number of steps. Clip gradients to handle explosion.
The LSTM adds a cell state with additive updates and learned gates (forget, input, output); the GRU is a lighter variant. The additive path lets gradients flow over long ranges.
A language model predicts the next token. Perplexity is exp(cross-entropy). Text is generated by sampling with a temperature, or by beam search.
An encoder–decoder maps one sequence to another but squeezes the source through a single vector. Attention removes that bottleneck.

problems.q: An LSTM has hidden size 128 and input size 64. Count the parameters (with biases) of one layer, and compare with a GRU layer of the same size.
problems.solution: LSTM: 4 × 128 × (128 + 64 + 1) = 4 × 128 × 193 = 98,816. GRU has three gate/candidate matrices: 3 × 128 × 193 = 74,112.

problems.q: An LSTM cell has c_{t−1} = −1, f = 0.5, i = 0.8, g = 0.6, o = 1. Compute c_t and h_t.
A language model gives the probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.1 and 0.2 to the four tokens of a sentence. Compute the perplexity of the sentence.

A scalar RNN has h_t = tanh(0.9 h_{t−1} + x_t). Estimate the influence of h₁ on h_{21} by the product of the weights, ignoring the tanh derivative, and say whether clipping or gating is the likelier fix if the weight were 1.2.
problems.solution: There are 20 factors: 0.9²⁰ = 0.12. With w = 1.2, 1.2²⁰ = 38.3, which explodes; gradient clipping addresses it. A weight below 1 loses the signal slowly (vanishing), which gating addresses.

problems.q: Logits (1, 0, −1) with temperature T = 2. Compute the softmax probabilities.
